source_text:
Confido enim vos bene exercitatos esse in sacris literis et nihil vos latet; mihi autem non est concessum. Modo, ut his scripturis dictum est, irascimini et nolite peccare, et sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram. Beatus, qui meminerit; quod ego credo esse in vobis.
Deus autem et pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, et ipse sempiternus pontifex, dei filius Iesus Christus, aedificet vos in fide et veritate et in omni mansuetudine et sine iracundia et in patientia et in longanimitate et tolerantia et castitate; et det vobis sortem et partem inter sanctos suos et nobis vobiscum et omnibus, qui sunt sub caelo, qui credituri sunt in dominum nostrum et deum Iesum Christum et in ipsius patrem, qui resuscitavit eum a mortuis.
Pro omnibus sanctis orate. Orate etiam pro regibus et potestatibus et principibus atque pro persequentibus et odientibus vos et pro inimicis crucis, ut fructus vester manifestus sit in omnibus, ut sitis in illo perfecti.
thought_title: Prayer for the Philippians' Growth and for All
orientation: Polycarp, writing in Latin, has just urged the Philippians to restore the fallen gently; now he expresses confidence in their knowledge of Scripture and prays for their growth and for all people.
pass_a_gloss: I am confident [that] you have been well trained in [the] sacred writings and nothing escapes you; but to me [it] has not been granted. Only, as [it] has been said in these scriptures, be angry and do not sin, and [the] sun must not set upon your anger. Blessed [is he] who will have remembered; which I believe to be in you. But God and [the] Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he himself [the] eternal high priest, God's son Jesus Christ, may he build you up in faith and truth and in all gentleness and without anger and in endurance and in long-suffering and tolerance and purity; and may he give to you a lot and a share among his saints and to us with you and to all who are under heaven, who are going to believe in our Lord and God Jesus Christ and in his Father, who raised him from [the] dead. For all [the] saints pray. Pray also for kings and powers and rulers and for [those] persecuting and hating you and for [the] enemies of [the] cross, so that your fruit may be manifest in all, so that you may be perfect in him.

choices.why: Renders the Latin phrase literally as 'sacred writings' rather than 'Scriptures' to preserve the source's descriptive wording.
Renders the Latin title literally; 'pontifex' is the high priest, and 'sempiternus' means eternal, matching the Christological title.
Uses the glossary term 'endurance' for patientia, which here corresponds to the Greek ὑπομονή in Polycarp's vocabulary.
Keeps the double expression literally; 'lot' and 'share' both render the idea of an allotted portion among the saints.
Renders the phrase literally; it echoes Paul's language in Philippians 3:18 about those who oppose the cross.
Keeps the agricultural metaphor of 'fruit' and the adjective 'manifest' literally, preserving the purpose clause's force.

bible_refs.note: sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram

pass_b_english: I am confident that you are well trained in the sacred writings and that nothing escapes you; this has not been granted to me. Only, as it is said in these scriptures, be angry and do not sin, and do not let the sun go down on your anger (Psalm 4:5 LXX; Ephesians 4:26). Blessed is the one who remembers this, and I believe it is true of you.

May God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ himself, the Son of God and eternal high priest, build you up in faith and truth, in all gentleness and freedom from anger, in endurance, long-suffering, forbearance, and purity. May he give you a lot and a share among his saints, and to us with you, and to all under heaven who are to believe in our Lord and God Jesus Christ and in his Father, who raised him from the dead.

Pray for all the saints. Pray also for kings and authorities and rulers, for those who persecute and hate you, and for the enemies of the cross, so that your fruit may be manifest in all things and you may be made perfect in him.

problems.why: The source says 'as it is said in these scriptures' (plural, referring to sacred writings). The English cites both Psalm 4:4 and Ephesians 4:26. However, 'irascimini et nolite peccare' is LXX Psalm 4:5 (Hebrew 4:4), and 'sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram' is Ephesians 4:26. The source introduces this as 'in these scriptures'—but the work brief says Psalm numbering follows LXX, so this should be 'Psalm 4:5 (LXX)' or similar. The English gives 'Psalm 4:4' which is Hebrew numbering, not LXX numbering as specified in brief. Also, the source presents both as 'scriptures' but Ephesians is NT, not LXX. The brief says 'Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and, where applicable, note LXX numbering (e.g., LXX Psalm numbering).' The English gives 'Psalm 4:4' without LXX notation, which contradicts the brief's requirement for LXX Psalm numbering.
problems.ruling: Brief requires LXX Psalm numbering; 'Psalm 4:4' uses Hebrew numbering, should be 'Psalm 4:5' per LXX.

fixed: Changed Psalm citation to LXX numbering per brief: source 'his scripturis' introduces both quotations; LXX Psalm 4:5 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 4:4.

problems.quote: church of God that sojourns at Philippi
problems.why: Same community called by three different labels across sections.

variants.text: church of God that sojourns at Philippi

problems.quote: May he give you a lot and a share among his saints
problems.why: 'A lot' likely means 'an allotment' or 'inheritance,' not the modern word 'lot.'
problems.fix: Render as 'a portion and a share' or 'an inheritance.'

problems.quote: be angry and do not sin, and do not let the sun go down on your anger (Psalm 4:5 LXX; Ephesians 4:26)
problems.why: Psalm 4:5 LXX says 'be angry and do not sin'; the second clause is from Ephesians only, not Psalm.
problems.fix: Separate citations: Psalm 4:5 LXX for first clause; Ephesians 4:26 for second.

Source 'sortem et partem' means 'a lot and a share'; 'lot' in English can mean a portion or allotment, but 'portion' is clearer and more natural here, so changed to 'a portion and a share'.
Source 'irascimini et nolite peccare' is Psalm 4:5 LXX; 'et sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram' is Ephesians 4:26, not Psalm. Separated the citations.

last_rejected.quote: this has not been granted to me
last_rejected.why: English 'this' is vague; Latin refers to being well-trained in scriptures. But 'this has not been granted to me' is a natural rendering of 'mihi autem non est concessum' in context. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: 'mihi autem non est concessum' naturally rendered 'this has not been granted to me'; context makes antecedent clear.

last_rejected.quote: and Jesus Christ himself, the Son of God and eternal high priest
last_rejected.source_quote: et ipse sempiternus pontifex, dei filius Iesus Christus
last_rejected.why: Latin word order: 'et ipse sempiternus pontifex, dei filius Iesus Christus' = 'and he himself [the] eternal high priest, God's son Jesus Christ'. English 'Jesus Christ himself, the Son of God and eternal high priest' changes word order but same meaning. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: Reordering 'et ipse sempiternus pontifex, dei filius Iesus Christus' preserves same meaning; no semantic loss.

last_rejected.why: 'credituri sunt' = 'who are going to believe' / 'who are to believe'. English correct. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: 'qui credituri sunt' = 'who are to believe'; English is accurate future participle rendering.

last_rejected.why: Latin 'et nobis vobiscum' = 'and to us with you' / 'and to us [together] with you'. English 'and to us with you' is slightly awkward but accurate. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: 'et nobis vobiscum' = 'and to us with you'; accurate dative rendering within normal range.

last_rejected.why: Latin 'fructus vester manifestus sit' = 'your fruit may be manifest/apparent'. English correct. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: 'fructus vester manifestus sit' = 'your fruit may be manifest'; English is accurate.

last_rejected.quote: you may be made perfect in him
last_rejected.why: Latin 'ut sitis in illo perfecti' = 'that you may be perfect in him'. English 'made perfect' adds passive causative nuance not in Latin ('sitis perfecti' = 'you may be perfect'). However, 'made perfect' is a common English idiom for 'perfected/complete'. The sense is very close. This is arguably within literary license. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: 'sitis perfecti' rendered 'be made perfect' is standard English idiom; no meaning changed.
